evidence_notes.research_design: Systematic review of 71 primary studies found through a DBLP title-keyword search and backward/forward snowballing, followed by two illustrative ChatDev case studies that repeatedly generated Snake and Tetris from fixed prompts with GPT-3.5-turbo at temperature 0.2.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: No matched single-agent comparison was run; single-agent and non-agent studies were explicitly excluded from the review. The two case studies held the prompt and ChatDev configuration constant across retries, but had no single-agent baseline, randomized conditions, automated acceptance suite, or inferential analysis.
headline_results: The review maps 71 studies across requirements engineering, code generation, quality assurance, maintenance, and end-to-end development, but does not estimate a causal multi-agent advantage over single agents.

Snake failed on the first attempt and became playable on the second; average development time was 76 seconds and average cost was $0.019 per attempt, and manual play indicated that the final game met the prompt requirements.
Tetris failed to produce functional gameplay in the first nine attempts; attempt 10 was playable but still lacked completed-row removal, with averages of 70 seconds and $0.020 per attempt.

The paper attributes potential gains to specialized roles, task decomposition, debate, peer review, testing, retrieval, and iterative feedback, while its own Tetris case prominently shows residual nondeterminism and requirement noncompliance.

The paper's autonomous, scalable, trustworthy Software Engineering 2.0 vision is aspirational; its direct empirical evidence is limited to two toy-game case studies rather than production deployment evidence.
limitations: The authors identify possible omission of relevant studies despite DBLP searching and snowballing.
Excluding single-agent studies prevents the review from supporting a controlled single-versus-multi conclusion.
The case studies cover only two small games, one model family, fixed prompts, manual functional inspection, and a small uncontrolled sequence of retries.
The Tetris result shows that repeated runs can remain incomplete even after ten attempts, so rapid generation and low per-attempt cost do not establish reliability.

The paper identifies communication bottlenecks, information overload, memory limits, inconsistent shared information, slow consensus, uncertain termination, and unresolved privacy under partial information as scaling barriers.
future_work: Identify role competencies and train or prompt agents against explicit software-engineering skill requirements.
Develop agent-oriented prompting languages with explicit behavior, task hierarchy, and communication semantics.
Build long-horizon collaborative benchmarks that measure communication efficiency, conflict handling, clarification, integration, peer review, and project outcomes.
Study hierarchical decomposition, prioritized communication, shared knowledge repositories, autonomous error handling, and scoped consensus for large projects.
Develop dynamic team sizing, role reassignment, resource allocation, monitoring, and stopping criteria.
Optimize human intervention points and apply access control, differential privacy, secure multi-party computation, federated learning, or homomorphic encryption to cross-organizational collaboration.
combinable_methods: Compiler, static-analysis, and test-framework feedback in iterative repair loops
Code-graph retrieval and shared blackboard or knowledge-repository memory
Human review at requirements, ethical, conflict, and system-validation gates
Hierarchical task decomposition with dynamic role and workflow generation
Cross-agent review, generated tests, debate, voting, and scoped consensus
Fine-grained authorization and privacy-preserving computation for shared data

quotes.use: Shows both nondeterminism under an unchanged prompt and eventual success on a moderately complex toy task.

quotes.use: Identifies communication overhead as a first-order scaling limit rather than assuming more agents always help.

quotes.use: Separates the proposed privacy mechanisms from current empirical maturity: the paper says the LMA-specific problem remains unsolved.

evidence_notes.research_design: Single-system case study of an LLM-driven audit over AEGIS's eight-file, approximately 7,152-line prompt-specification surface for nine audit-and-fix rounds, plus a blinded four-vendor, three-run-per-vendor partial replication on a 114-line synthetic fixture with five seeded defects and an 18-defect inter-rater subsample.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: No single-agent or human-review baseline and no initial full-scope one-pass control were run. The production surface was stable except for targeted fixes, but audit scope expanded from single-file to full-scope and the protocol co-evolved. The synthetic audit held the fixture, checklist, output schema, and hidden gold labels constant across 12 traces; temperature was zero where supported and otherwise provider default.
headline_results: Nine rounds surfaced 51 defects with per-round counts 15, 8, 12, 2, 8, 1, 4, 1, and 0; the observed trend was non-monotonic and ended after one clean pass.
A Mann-Kendall test reported S = -26, Z = -2.64, p = 0.008, and Kendall's tau = -0.72, but rounds were dependent and the changing audit protocol confounded interpretation.

On the seeded fixture, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro found all five defects in every run, Claude found all five in two of three runs, Grok found four in every run, and the multi-vendor union found all five; average spurious findings ranged from 0 to 1.3 per run.

On the 18-defect subsample, category agreement was Cohen's kappa 0.801 (95% CI 0.564 to 1.000), while severity agreement was 0.458 (95% CI 0.008 to 0.811), showing materially weaker reliability for severity judgments.

AEGIS is described as production-deployed, but this study measures specification consistency only; it does not show that correcting the 51 defects improved runtime performance, reliability, security, or operational outcomes.
limitations: The production case has n = 1, no control group, a post hoc taxonomy, and a Claude-family inspector auditing specifications authored by the same model family.
Protocol maturation and remediation occurred together, so falling defect counts cannot isolate audit effectiveness from expanded coverage or sequence effects.
One stochastic clean pass does not establish a fixed point or correctness; no repeat trials were run per production round.
The public fixture is roughly thirty times smaller and deliberately has higher defect density, so it validates the method but not production-scale counts or convergence.
The cross-vendor replication is neither multi-system nor human-only/hybrid, and it does not bound shared-model blind spots on the private production specifications.
The author-coded taxonomy is only partially replicated by an LLM-panel modal coder; no human second coder was used.
future_work: Run multi-system replications on independent specification surfaces.
Compare iterative full-scope auditing with a locked single-pass full-scope control.
Add human-only and hybrid human-LLM review arms and a human second coder.
Lock model version, decoding settings, and full-scope protocol before remediation; repeat each round to estimate auditor variance.
Require two consecutive clean full-scope passes and tie specification fixes to downstream runtime and operational metrics.
combinable_methods: Locked cross-document checklist and structured finding schema
Cross-vendor audit panels to reduce correlated blind spots
Human inspection and inter-rater validation
Verification greps for structural checks plus semantic LLM review
Runtime tests, adversarial testing, and operational metrics after specification repair
Two-consecutive-clean-pass stopping rules with repeat-trial audits

quotes.text: A single-pass full-scope control was not run.
quotes.use: Directly records the missing comparison needed to attribute gains to iteration rather than full-scope visibility.

quotes.text:
OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 and Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro each detected all five seeded
defects in every run; the re-baselined Claude detected all five in two of three runs; xAI’s

Scope:This is a partial replication, bounded in three specific ways. First, it is not
a multi-systemreplication: running the protocol on additional independent specification

quotes.use: Prevents extrapolating a synthetic cross-vendor result into broad or production-system validity.

quotes.text:
Construct:Convergence to zero findings does not establish correctness, only internal
consistency under the locked protocol’s coverage. Runtime validation remains a necessary
complementary quality gate; we report nothing about runtime behaviour here.
quotes.use: Defines the assurance boundary and supports combining specification audit with executable validation.

evidence_notes.research_design: MAFBench controlled benchmark study spanning framework overhead, MemoryAgentBench, three planning benchmarks across seven LLMs, five CatDB specialization tasks, and AGENTSNET coordination tasks over multiple topology classes and agent counts from 4 to 100. A direct LLM call was included for a 50-trial trivial-query overhead experiment.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: Models, prompts, tasks, data, scoring, concurrency or stopping criteria were fixed within each experiment while one architecture dimension varied. This supports local causal comparisons of interfaces and topologies. It does not provide a matched single-agent-versus-specialized-multi-agent comparison on an end-to-end software task: the direct baseline is a trivial query, specialization varies conditioning on an agent, and coordination compares only multi-agent topologies.
headline_results: For the trivial fixed query, direct calls had 0.38-second median latency and 8.88 requests/second, while Concordia had 44.47-second median latency and 0.089 requests/second, approximately 117 times the median latency.

Retrieval-only LangGraph had the best overall memory score at 23.8; bounded hybrid memory led accurate retrieval and test-time learning, while multi-hop selective forgetting remained below 5 across all architectures.

Schema-constrained planning could reduce accuracy sharply: Qwen-7B fell from 13.0% to 3.4% on GSM8K and had 84.7% formatting failure; Crew planning exceeded 30 times baseline runtime for Llama-3.1-8B on CSQA, while free-form planning had zero formatting failures in the reported comparison.

Professional role labels produced no consistent gain over no role; expert procedural guidance raised Yelp F1 from approximately 41.9 to as high as 100 under otherwise fixed data, model, task, and prompt structure.

Communication geometry was task-dependent: sparse structures worked well for local tasks, while only fully connected communication consistently solved global consensus at every scale, in three rounds; no topology was robust across all tasks.

Production-oriented design guidance is inferred from controlled and mostly synthetic benchmarks; no production deployment, end-to-end SDLC outcome, security evaluation, or quantitative tool-use result is reported.
limitations: The paper is an arXiv preprint and does not report production-system validation.
The appendix explicitly describes memory comparison as an architectural disclosure rather than strict equivalence or full normalization across implementations.
Quantitative tool-use evaluation is deferred because frameworks largely delegate function calling to the model/provider.
Most evaluations use trivial, reasoning, tabular-ML, memory, or abstract coordination tasks rather than software-development projects.
Repeat counts and statistical uncertainty are not reported consistently outside the 50-trial overhead experiment.
Security, governance, code quality, and operational failure recovery are not evaluated.
future_work: Add explicit memory editing, dependency-aware deletion, contradiction resolution, and bounded growth guarantees.
Version, audit, revert, and validate procedural specialist knowledge across its lifecycle.
Support online topology reconfiguration with explicit convergence, stability, correctness, and cost guarantees.
Automate compilation of task requirements and deployment constraints into cost-aware orchestration, memory, planning, specialization, and coordination architectures.
Evaluate framework-controlled tool selection and execution once architectures expose those mechanisms.
combinable_methods: Retrieval-first memory with bounded short-term accumulation
Permissive free-form planning with lightweight validation
Expert procedural templates rather than role labels alone
Task-specific communication topology and adaptive graph selection
Shallow orchestration selected under explicit latency and throughput budgets
Automated architecture search and cost-aware system compilation

quotes.text:

aligns execution and measurement protocols to isolate the impact

abstraction, and communication structure, across both single-agent
and multi-agent settings. We fix the underlying LLM to control for
model effects and attribute observed differences to the framework
architecture.
quotes.use: Documents the study's strongest within-experiment controls and the intended level of causal attribution.

We do not report quantitative
tool-use results because current frameworks delegate tool invocation
entirely to the LLM via native function-calling interfaces, without
architectural control over tool selection or execution.
quotes.use: Marks an important empirical gap for production software agents that depend on tools.

Table 9 shows that schema-constrained planning reduces accuracy

quotes.use: Shows that additional orchestration can be harmful and that interface design, not merely extra planning, controls the outcome.

evidence_notes.research_design: Tool paper with initial controlled validation on a minimal Planner-to-Coder workflow and ChatDev. Both used 30 ProgramDev tasks, five executions per condition, and three conditions: fault-free baseline, one 1,000-ms delay at the first planning LLM call, and one 1,000-ms delay at the Planner-to-Coder handoff. The principal metric was end-to-end latency amplification divided by injected delay.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: Within each target system the benchmark, task set, repetition count, fault location, and delay magnitude were fixed. There is no single-agent baseline, no matched single-versus-multi quality comparison, and no evidence that model, prompt, tools, or workflow were equivalent between the demo and ChatDev. Raw baseline latency and task-success effects are not reported.
headline_results: In the demo, a 1-second LLM delay produced mean/median amplification of 1.053/1.036, while the A2A delay produced 1.295/1.390.
In ChatDev, a single 1-second LLM delay produced mean/median amplification of 48.1/13.9, and an A2A delay produced 59.2/6.6, indicating large and highly skewed downstream latency effects.
The tool aligns OpenTelemetry spans for sessions, workflow segments, agent steps, A2A messages, tools, LLM calls, and injected faults, enabling baseline/faulty trace comparison.
The paper demonstrates observability of injected latency propagation, not improved correctness, recovery, or specialized-agent advantage.
Framework agnosticism and practical usefulness are design claims supported by only a demo and one research framework; production readiness is not empirically evaluated.
limitations: Validation covers two systems and only fixed delays, despite the implementation listing drop, timeout, rate-limit, network-error, malformed-response, and tool faults.
The study reports latency amplification without task success, output quality, recovery rate, confidence intervals, or significance tests.
The gap between ChatDev means and medians indicates strong skew or outliers that are not analyzed.
Users must manually annotate workflow boundaries, and portability beyond the two targets is not measured.
The current tool lacks paired-run differencing, trace summarization, root-cause ranking, and automated debugging reports.
No production deployment, security fault campaign, or single-agent comparison is reported.
future_work: Add workflow-level, memory-related, and coordination faults and broader injection surfaces.
Build paired-run differencing, trace summarization, root-cause ranking, and automated debugging reports over the trace layer.
Evaluate whether observed faults change task quality and whether systems recover, not only how latency propagates.
Validate integration cost and behavior across more frameworks and production workflows.
combinable_methods: OpenTelemetry distributed tracing across agent, message, tool, and model boundaries
Configuration-driven A2A, tool-call, and LLM-call fault injection
Paired baseline-versus-faulty execution with trace-aligned artifacts
Offline message hashes and previews for handoff inspection
Task-success, correctness, recovery, and cost metrics layered over traces

quotes.text:
The difficulty is not only that the workflows are multi-step
and distributed across agents, but also that they are stochastic:
the same task can unfold differently across runs. As a result,
simple logs or final success rates are often not enough to
understand what happened or to compare normal and faulty
executions in a principled way.
quotes.use: Motivates process-level observability as a complement to final-output metrics for nondeterministic agent systems.

quotes.text:
In both cases, we

msinjected at the first LLM call in the planning phase, and a

quotes.use: Records the exact within-system controls, repetition count, and perturbations used in validation.

quotes.text:
In particular, injecting a single LLM delay yields a mean

quotes.use: Quantifies how a small localized delay can be magnified in a message-heavy multi-agent workflow.

evidence_notes.research_design: MAS-FIRE derives 15 semantic and coordination fault types and injects them through prompt modification, response rewriting, or message-routing manipulation. It evaluates MetaGPT on 164 HumanEval tasks, Table-Critic on 400 WikiTableQuestions tasks, and Camel on 251 WebShop tasks, each with GPT-5 and DeepSeek-V3 at Pass@1; GPT-5-mini generated semantic faults. Four authors used grounded theory to derive behaviors, and a GPT-5 annotator achieved reported Cohen's kappa 0.94 against a held-out human set.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: Within a given MAS, fault-free and injected execution and the GPT-5/DeepSeek-V3 model pair provide controlled comparisons. No single-agent baseline is reported. Cross-architecture claims are not matched: the three MAS use different domains, datasets, workflows, tools, baseline rates, and applicable faults; all evaluations are single-trial, and communication faults could be injected only into MetaGPT.
headline_results: MetaGPT's shared message pool was associated with more than 90% robustness under critical-information loss versus about 67% for Camel, and Table-Critic retained more than 89% under planning faults versus MetaGPT as low as 43.84%; these cross-system differences are also task- and implementation-confounded.
Configuration and instruction faults were most damaging: MetaGPT reached 0.0% to 31.68% robustness under Blind Trust and Role Ambiguity, and instruction faults reduced it to at most 13.7%.

The strongest contrary finding was Blind Trust in Table-Critic: GPT-5 robustness was 6.32% versus DeepSeek-V3 at 70.61%, a 64.29-point advantage for the weaker model attributed to less strict compliance with the corrupted directive.
MetaGPT maintained greater than 93% robustness under communication faults through hard-coded filtering, deduplication, and cycle detection; the other systems could not receive those injections.

Mechanism-level retries/parsers and rule-based filters achieved high local recovery for structural faults, but semantically valid hallucination, conflict, and ambiguity required reasoning-level detection and sometimes a clarification channel.

The paper motivates production hardening, but all evidence comes from benchmark fault injection rather than production deployment; cost, latency, real adversaries, and a matched single-agent comparison are not evaluated.
limitations: The paper has no dedicated threats-to-validity section or explicit limitations discussion.
Cross-architecture comparisons conflate topology with benchmark, task type, implementation, tool environment, baseline success, and fault applicability.
All reported task evaluations are single-trial Pass@1, so nondeterministic variance is not estimated.
The 1% of semantic injections rejected by integrity checks were rerun, and some tool tasks were excluded, which may condition the evaluated fault set.
GPT-5-mini both constructs realistic semantic perturbations and GPT-5 later scales taxonomy annotation, introducing model-mediated measurement dependencies.
There is no single-agent, human-team, production, latency, token-cost, or security-attack baseline.
future_work: Implement conditional compliance so agents challenge corrupted or contradictory upstream instructions before irreversible actions.
Add multi-source validation from independent agents or environmental ground truth.
Insert lightweight schema and semantic verification checkpoints between linear pipeline stages, with targeted re-execution.
Replicate topology comparisons on the same tasks, models, tools, prompts, fault set, and repeated trials, including a single-agent arm.
Evaluate production traces, adversarial security faults, and cost-latency-reliability tradeoffs.
combinable_methods: Shared message pools for recoverable historical context
Iterative critic-refiner loops and independent validator agents
Deterministic parsers, retries, message deduplication, and cycle detection
Conditional compliance and proactive human clarification
Multi-source validation, debate, voting, and environmental re-perception
Inline schema, semantic, tool, and test checkpoints
Process-level fault occurrence, local-recovery, and end-to-end success metrics

quotes.text:
For each MAS, we select task datasets representative of its tar-
get domain. MetaGPT is evaluated onHumanEval[ 55], a bench-
mark for functional correctness of generated code. Table-Critic
is evaluated onWikiTableQuestions[ 31], a dataset requiring
complex table reasoning and multi-step inference. Camel is eval-
uated onWebShop[ 57], which requires multi-turn interaction
and decision-making in simulated e-commerce environments.
quotes.use: Shows why the reported architecture differences are not matched topology ablations: each system is evaluated on a different task domain.

quotes.text: Note:All evaluations aresingle-trial (Pass@1).
quotes.use: Identifies the absence of repeated trials for systems whose central reliability problem is nondeterminism.

quotes.text:
Notably,Blind Trustreveals a paradox: Table-Critic
with GPT-5 achieves only 𝑅𝑆 𝑓 = 6.32%, while DeepSeek-V3 main-
tains 𝑅𝑆 𝑓 = 70.61%, there is a64.29%gap favoring the weaker model
due to stricter instruction adherence preventing recovery (detailed
in Sec. 5.2).
quotes.use: Prominently records a contrary result in which stronger model capability sharply worsened fault tolerance.

quotes.text:
Communication faultsrepresent the least destructive threat
category, consistently yielding RS>93%in MetaGPT. Other MAS
frameworks were excluded as they lack a communication mod-
ule, preventing the injection ofCommunication Faults.
quotes.use: Supports deterministic communication defenses while exposing restricted fault applicability across architectures.

quotes.text:
The core vulnerability is single-path dependency: no redundancy
exists to catch semantic drift before it reaches downstream con-
sumers. We identify two complementary mitigation strategies. First,
multi-source validation: downstream agents should reconcile infor-
mation from multiple independent sources, such as parallel agent
interpretations or environmental ground truth, to detect inconsis-
tencies before acting. Second,inline verification checkpoints: light-
weight validation stages between pipeline steps can assess output
plausibility (e.g., schema conformance, semantic consistency with
the task specification) and trigger re-execution when anomalies are
detected.
quotes.use: Gives concrete complementary controls for preserving specialist decomposition without unchecked error propagation.

evidence_notes.research_design: Qualitative mapping study of 94 LLM-based multi-agent software-engineering papers collected from two prior surveys and an arXiv cs.SE search through 30 September 2024. The first author manually extracted task, ISO/IEC 25010 quality attributes, design patterns, and rationales; two coauthors reviewed results and resolved disagreements through discussion. Open coding and constant comparison were used for new pattern and rationale categories.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: No experimental manipulation, direct single-versus-multi comparison, effect-size synthesis, or re-evaluation of primary-study outputs was performed. Frequencies show what source authors considered or used, not whether a pattern caused better outcomes under matched requirements, prompts, tools, and models.
headline_results: Code generation accounts for 45 of 94 studies (47.9%); only 7 cover end-to-end development (7.4%) and 8 end-to-end maintenance (8.5%).

Quality attention is uneven: functional suitability appears in 89 studies (94.7%), performance efficiency in 48 (51.1%), maintainability in 47 (50.0%), reliability in 34 (36.2%), security in 10 (10.6%), and interaction capability in 9 (9.6%).

Role-Based Cooperation appears in 44 studies (46.8%) and Self-Reflection in 34 (36.2%), while Human-Reflection appears in 5, Agent Evaluator in 3, Debate-Based Cooperation in 4, and Voting-Based Cooperation in 3.
The review identifies a production-readiness gap: no widely accepted end-to-end benchmark, incomplete lifecycle metrics, and difficult cross-stage artifact consistency.
A contrary result reported from one included empirical study found no apparent output-performance difference between one-pass and multi-pass prompting, while one-pass used fewer API calls.
The study supports modular specialist roles as a maintainability pattern, but does not empirically demonstrate that specialization outperforms a matched single agent.
limitations: The authors state that manual collection and extraction risk individual bias; a pilot, coauthor review, and consensus discussions mitigate but do not quantify it.
The source corpus derives from two prior surveys and arXiv, so coverage and publication quality may constrain external validity.
The study explicitly does not support causal inference and reports no inter-rater statistic.
Counts reflect mentions and design intentions rather than validated quality attainment or production operation.
The paper inconsistently reports Role-Based Cooperation as 46.8% and 47.4%, and Self-Reflection as 36.2% and 35.8%; the raw counts 44 and 34 over 94 correspond to 46.8% and 36.2%.
End-to-end studies are sparse and lack common lifecycle benchmarks or assured handoff semantics.
future_work: Develop comprehensive end-to-end criteria and benchmarks spanning requirements, architecture, implementation, testing, and maintenance.
Validate cross-stage artifact contracts and consistency rather than evaluating stages independently.
Balance performance efficiency with maintainability through narrow roles and escalation to expensive high-assurance procedures only for difficult cases.
Use iterative human-in-the-loop evaluation to address expectation mismatch, ambiguous communication, and weak interaction validation.
Increase empirical attention to security, integrity, operability, analysability, and sustained lifecycle behavior.
combinable_methods: Role-based cooperation with explicit responsibilities and interfaces
Self-reflection and peer cross-reflection
Tool registries, adapters, and retrieval-augmented generation
Human reflection and independent agent evaluators
Debate, voting, multi-path planning, and hierarchical escalation
Execution feedback, automated tests, and acceptance criteria
Quality-attribute tradeoff analysis for efficiency, maintainability, reliability, and security

quotes.text:

MAS for SE tasks.

quotes.text:
Results show thatRole-Based
Cooperation(46.8%) is the most frequently used design pattern by the designers of LLM-based
MASs.Self-Reflection(36.2%) is also widely used in designing LLM-based MASs for SE tasks.
quotes.use: Identifies the dominant specialist-agent and iterative-reflection patterns in the mapped literature.

quotes.text:
Although benchmarks for code generation exist and recent initiatives like DevBench [20]
have begun to address multiple stages of the software lifecycle, there is still no widely accepted
benchmark that can evaluate MASs across the entire development lifecycle in a comprehensive
manner. Third, ensuring consistency of generated artifacts across stages is inherently difficult.
quotes.use: Shows that asserted end-to-end automation is not backed by standardized lifecycle-wide evaluation or reliable handoffs.

quotes.text:
They also compared different prompt settings, and found that one-pass and multi-pass
prompting have no apparent performance differences in generating outputs. However, one-pass
prompting consumes fewer API calls, making it more resource-efficient.
quotes.use: Preserves a contrary finding that extra iterative coordination can add cost without an apparent output gain.

evidence_notes.research_design: Multi-vocal literature review of 114 sources: 74 peer-reviewed studies and 40 grey-literature sources. Searches retrieved 1,874 academic and 482 grey records, followed by staged screening, snowballing, quality assessment, descriptive statistics, and thematic coding of motivations, models, benchmarks, challenges, solutions, and future work.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: No meta-analysis or matched single-agent-versus-multi-agent synthesis was performed. Primary studies varied in prompts, temperatures, Pass@k definitions, tools, models, tasks, and architectures; the review explicitly notes that these variations weaken comparability. Only 29 of 114 sources supplied adoption reasons and 52 used benchmarks, so broad benefit statements are not universal evidence.
headline_results: Only 29 of 114 studies (25.4%) reported reasons for using agents; performance enhancement appeared in 12 (10.5%), complex-task handling in 9 (7.9%), operational efficiency/scalability in 7 (6.1%), and team collaboration in 6 (5.3%).

Fifty-two studies (45.61%) used one or more of 37 identified benchmarks; HumanEval appeared in 29 and MBPP in 18, showing dominant function-level, unit-test-based evaluation rather than production-scale evidence.

Security evaluation was rare: RedCode and LLMSecEval each appeared in one study. Security/privacy challenges were reported by 11 of 114 sources, computational/resource constraints by 15, memory limitations by 11, verification challenges by 9, and prompt challenges by 6.
The corpus contained 57 closed-source-model uses and 26 open-source-model uses; GPT-series models accounted for 43, creating provider dependence, temporal reproducibility, privacy, and cost concerns.

The review characterizes the field as advanced prototyping or early consolidation, with high architectural heterogeneity, narrow benchmarks, proprietary-model dependence, weak reporting, and limited deployment validation.

Claims that multi-agent systems improve over single models are synthesized qualitatively from heterogeneous sources; the review does not recover or aggregate matched controls, effect sizes, ablations, or costs sufficient to establish when specialization itself causes an advantage.
limitations: The authors acknowledge possible missed studies, selection and coding bias, and subjective thematic interpretation despite multi-author review.
Grey literature has weaker quality control and may include vested interests; some industrial results rely on proprietary datasets and organization-specific workflows.
Primary-study protocol variation in prompts, temperature, Pass@k, tools, and model versions limits cross-study comparison.
Earlier or proprietary model APIs cannot be exactly reproduced and may not generalize to current models.
The review reports frequencies rather than effect sizes or evidence-strength-weighted conclusions, and it does not isolate single-versus-multi causality.

Academic evaluation is structurally misaligned with claimed complexity and industrial needs: small function tasks emphasize correctness while security, compliance, cost, maintainability, collaboration, and long-horizon behavior remain sparse.
future_work: Create realistic long-horizon, repository-level, multimodal, security-aware, and collaboration-aware benchmarks with failure and cost metrics.
Develop adaptive, token-efficient orchestration, selective communication, dynamic team sizing, and resource-performance studies in industrial settings.
Integrate privacy-preserving computation, role-based permissions, trust management, sandboxing, DLP, secret handling, audit logging, and security-specialist agents.
Build structured and scalable memory with revision, compression, multimodal context, and long-range dependency support.
Adopt hybrid human-agent workflows in which people guide, validate, and make strategic decisions.
Standardize reporting of prompts, model versions, configurations, coordination, latency, tokens, and deployment constraints.
combinable_methods: Schema-based communication and explicit component ownership
Iterative feedback plus traditional static analysis, symbolic reasoning, tests, and validation layers
Sandboxed execution, monitoring, DLP, audit logs, credentials controls, and security benchmarks
Local open-source or smaller specialist models for privacy and cost control
External retrieval memory with selective context and compression
Human-in-the-loop review and decision gates
Repository-level and agent-communication benchmarks with resource and failure metrics
